passage_text:
Researchers at the Institute for Cognitive Enhancement examined the effects of two novel mnemonic techniques on short‑term memory retention. Participants (N = 120) were randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) Control (no mnemonic training), (2) Technique A (the method of loci), (3) Technique B (semantic clustering), and (4) Combined (both techniques applied sequentially). Each participant was given a list of 20 unrelated words to memorize and then tested immediately and again after a 30‑minute delay. The table below summarizes the mean recall scores (out of 20) and standard deviations for each group at the two time points.

Table: Mean Recall Scores by Group and Time Point

| Group      | Time Point | Mean Score | SD |
|------------|------------|------------|----|
| Control    | Immediate  | 10.2       | 2.5 |
| Control    | Delayed    | 8.7        | 2.8 |
| Technique A| Immediate  | 13.5       | 2.1 |
| Technique A| Delayed    | 11.9       | 2.4 |
| Technique B| Immediate  | 12.8       | 2.3 |
| Technique B| Delayed    | 11.2       | 2.6 |
| Combined   | Immediate  | 15.4       | 1.9 |
| Combined   | Delayed    | 13.7       | 2.0 |

The researchers hypothesized that mnemonic training would improve both immediate and delayed recall, with the combined approach yielding the greatest benefit. They also noted that the standard deviations were smaller in the combined group, suggesting more consistent performance among participants who used both techniques.
stem: Based on the data presented, which statement most accurately reflects the effect of mnemonic training on delayed recall?

options.A: Technique A produced the greatest improvement in delayed recall compared to the Control group.
options.B: The Combined group had the highest mean delayed recall, higher than Control and each single technique.
options.C: Technique B outperformed Technique A in delayed recall, but both were still inferior to the Control group.
options.D: All mnemonic techniques resulted in identical delayed recall scores, suggesting no effect.

explanation: Correct: B. Mean delayed recall was 13.7 for Combined, versus 11.9 (A), 11.2 (B) and 8.7 (Control). Why the others are wrong: A) Technique A gained 3.2 words over Control, but Combined gained 5.0, which is larger. C) Technique B (11.2) scored lower than A (11.9) and both scored above Control (8.7). D) The delayed means range from 8.7 to 13.7 and are not identical.
trap: Choosing a single technique as best without comparing it with the Combined group.

stem: Which feature of the study design best supports attributing group differences in recall to the training rather than to pre-existing differences among participants?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to the four groups
options.B: Testing recall both immediately and after 30 minutes
options.C: Use of a 20-word list of unrelated words
options.D: The smaller standard deviation in the Combined group

explanation: Correct: A. Random assignment balances known and unknown participant characteristics across groups, so group differences can be attributed to the intervention. Why the others are wrong: B) Two time points describe retention over time but do not equalize groups. C) A standard word list makes the task uniform but does not balance participant characteristics. D) The SD describes spread within a group and has no role in group comparability.
trap: Mistaking repeated measurement or standardized materials for control of confounding.

stem: Calculate the difference in forgetting (immediate minus delayed recall) between the Combined group and the Control group.
explanation: Control forgetting = 10.2 - 8.7 = 1.5 words. Combined forgetting = 15.4 - 13.7 = 1.7 words. Difference = 1.7 - 1.5 = 0.2 words (the Combined group forgot slightly more in absolute terms despite higher scores).
trap: Stopping at a single group's forgetting score (1.5 or 1.7 words) instead of subtracting Control forgetting from Combined forgetting.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the table?

options.A: The Combined group had the smallest SD of the four groups at both time points.
options.B: Mean recall was lower at the delayed test than at the immediate test in every group.
options.C: Immediate recall in the Combined group exceeded that of the Control group by 5.2 words.
options.D: The smaller SD in the Combined group shows that the Combined technique is more effective than either single technique.

explanation: Correct: D. The SD measures spread of scores around a group mean, not effectiveness; effectiveness is judged by the means. Why the others are wrong: A) The Combined SDs (1.9 and 2.0) are below all other SDs (2.1 to 2.8), so A is supported. B) Delayed means are lower in all groups (8.7 vs 10.2, 11.9 vs 13.5, 11.2 vs 12.8, 13.7 vs 15.4), so B is supported. C) 15.4 - 10.2 = 5.2, so C is supported.
trap: Treating a smaller SD as evidence of a better technique.

stem: By how many words did mean delayed recall in the Combined group exceed that of the better single-technique group?
explanation: Correct: A. The better single technique at delay is Technique A (11.9), so 13.7 - 11.9 = 1.8 words. Why the others are wrong: B) 2.5 is the difference from Technique B (13.7 - 11.2), which is not the better single technique. C) 5.0 is the difference from Control (13.7 - 8.7). D) 1.7 is the Combined immediate-minus-delayed forgetting (15.4 - 13.7), not a group difference.
trap: Comparing with Control or with the weaker single technique instead of the better one.
